"Ran YanSchool of Mathematics and Statistics, Tianshui Normal University, Tianshui 741001, ChinaXiaolei ZhangCorresponding authorSchool of Mathematics and Statistics, Tianshui Normal University, Tianshui 741001, China
Abstract
Let S be an isosimple module, that is, a nonzero module isomorphic to every nonzero submodule of itself. In this paper, we investigate if the square S2:=S⊕S is isoartinian when S is an isosimple module. If the base ring is commutative, then the answer is yes. However, for noncommutative rings this is no longer true even when EndR⁡(S) is a discrete valuation ring. We also give some positive results coming from quasi-projectivity and Morita equivalence. Finally, we consider when every finite powers of an isosimple module are isoartinian provided it holds for the square. Our related result says that if S2 is isoartinian and E=EndR⁡(S) is either commutative Noetherian or right semihereditary, then every finite power of S is isoartinian.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 16D70, 16D40, 16P70.
Keywords. Isosimple module; Isoartinian module; Quasi-projective module; Endomorphism ring; Reflexive module.
1Introduction and Preliminaries

Introduction
Recall that a nonzero module is called simple if it has no nonzero proper submodules. A module is called artinian if every descending chain of its submodules eventually becomes stationary. These are basic notions in the structure theory of modules. Every simple module is artinian, and every finite direct sum of simple modules is artinian [1, 11]. The notions of isosimplicity and isoartinianity arise by replacing equality of submodules by isomorphism. A nonzero module S is isosimple if every nonzero submodule of S is isomorphic to S. A module M is isoartinian if, for every descending chainM0⊇M1⊇M2⊇⋯of submodules of M, there is an integer d≥0 such that Mi≅Md for all i≥d. Thus the submodules need not eventually be equal; only their isomorphism types must stabilize. Every simple module is isosimple, every artinian module is isoartinian, and every isosimple module is isoartinian.Facchini and Nazemian studied chain conditions up to isomorphism in [7, 8] and developed further aspects of the theory in [9]. Their work connects these conditions with generalizations of classical module structure, including the isoradical and modules generated by isosimple modules. Isosimple modules also appear under the name virtually simple modules in [3, 4]. A module is called virtually semisimple if each of its submodules is isomorphic to a direct summand. These related notions lead to versions of familiar decomposition questions in which isomorphism replaces equality. However, their direct-sum properties do not follow formally from those of simple or semisimple modules.The fact that finite direct sums of simple modules are artinian suggests asking whether direct sums of isosimple modules satisfy the corresponding chain condition up to isomorphism. Facchini and Nazemian formulated this question in [9, Open Problems (2)]:Is a direct sum of isosimple modules an isoartinian module?In this paper, we settle the question negatively. We give a commutative example in which a direct sum of two nonisomorphic isosimple modules is not isoartinian. We then prove that, over a noncommutative ring, failure can occur even for two copies of the same module. Thus the more restrictive questionS​ isosimple⟹S2:=S⊕S​ isoartinian​?(1)also has a negative answer in general. Our counterexample has a faithful isosimple module over a complete local prime ring that is Noetherian on both sides. Moreover, the endomorphism ring of the module is a commutative discrete valuation ring.The contents of the paper are as follows. Section 2 classifies isosimple modules over commutative rings: they are precisely the modules R/𝔭 for which R/𝔭 is a principal ideal domain. Consequently, all their finite powers are isoartinian. Section 3 gives a counterexample of (1) even when EndR⁡(S) is a discrete valuation ring. Section 4 proves that quasi-projective isosimple modules have isoartinian finite powers. Morita equivalence preserves the relevant properties and gives examples over matrix rings over principal right ideal domains. We also show that quasi-projectivity is not necessary. Finally, Section 5 considers whetherS2​ isoartinian⟹Sn​ isoartinian for every positive integer ​n.(2)The square hypothesis implies that SE is flat and that every N≤Sn has the form M⊗ES, with M≤En finitely generated. We prove the implication when E is commutative Noetherian or right semihereditary.All rings have identity, and all modules are unital. Unless otherwise stated, modules are right modules. Let R be a ring and S be always an isosimple R-module. We write Sn for a finite direct sum, and E=EndR⁡(S). Thus S is a left E-module, and HomR⁡(S,N) is a right E-module. By a principal right ideal domain we mean a domain in which every right ideal is principal.
Preliminaries
We include the elementary properties on isosimple modules and isoartinian modules. Uniform dimension, essential submodules, and the Hopfian property are used in the usual sense [1, 11]. The role of finite uniform dimension in quotient-ring theory goes back to Goldie [10].Lemma 1.1.
An isosimple module S is cyclic, Noetherian and uniform. Every nonzero endomorphism of S is injective. Its endomorphism ring is a right Ore domain, andfE⊆gE⟺fS⊆gS.The intersection of two nonzero principal right ideals of E is principal.Proof.
Pick 0≠s∈S. Since s​R≅S, the module S is cyclic. Hence every submodule is either zero or cyclic, so S is Noetherian. If f≠0, then an isomorphism f​S→S composed with f gives a surjective endomorphism of the Noetherian module S. It must be injective, so f is injective.If nonzero submodules U,V had zero intersection, choose f with image U. Then V,f​V,f2​V,… form a direct sum: V∩f​S=0, and injectivity of f gives the claim by induction. Their finite partial sums contradict the ascending chain condition. Therefore S is uniform.The factorization statement follows by using the inverse of the isomorphism g:S→g​S. If f,g≠0, write f​S∩g​S=h​S with h≠0. Factoring through f and g gives h=f​a=g​b, and the same argument for any element of f​E∩g​E shows that this intersection is h​E. This also proves the right Ore condition. ∎Corollary 1.2.
If EndR⁡(S) is commutative, then it is a UFD.Proof.
Lemma 1.1 gives least common multiples as intersections of principal ideals. In a commutative domain this is the same as the GCD property. The correspondence f​E↔f​S gives the ascending chain condition on principal ideals. A GCD domain with this condition is a UFD; this is the usual factorization criterion [5]. ∎Lemma 1.3.
Every nonzero submodule N≤Sn embeds, under some coordinate projection, as an essential submodule of Sr, where r=u.dim⁡N≤n.Proof.
Choose a set of coordinates of smallest possible size such that the projection onto them is injective on N, and let L≤Sr be its image. Removing any coordinate destroys injectivity. Therefore L has nonzero intersection with every coordinate axis. These intersections form an essential submodule of Sr, because each coordinate is uniform. Hence L≤essSr, and its uniform dimension is r. ∎Proposition 1.4.
For every positive integer n, the following are equivalent:
(i)Sn is isoartinian;
(ii)every submodule of Sn is isomorphic to Sr for some 0≤r≤n.If these conditions hold, then every essential submodule of Sn is isomorphic to Sn.Proof.

Conversely, under (ii) the integers u.dim⁡Mi in any descending chain eventually stabilize. The corresponding powers of S are then isomorphic, so the chain stabilizes up to isomorphism. ∎Remark 1.5.
The criterion uses essential submodules and coordinate projections, not cancellation of arbitrary summands. In particular, a nonsplit short exact sequence cannot be treated as a direct-sum decomposition.
2The commutative case
In this section, we will show that the square S2 is always isoartinian when S is an isosimple module over a commutative ring.Theorem 2.1.
Let R be commutative and S≠0 a right R-module. The following are equivalent:
(i)S is isosimple;
(ii)there is a prime ideal 𝔭 such that R/𝔭 is a principal ideal domain and S≅R/𝔭.In this case every finite power Sn is isoartinian.Proof.
Assume S is isosimple. By Lemma 1.1, S≅R/I for some ideal I. Put D=R/I. Endomorphisms of the cyclic module S are given by multiplication by elements of D, so D≅EndR⁡(S) is a domain. Every nonzero ideal J of D is isomorphic to D. If θ:D→J is an isomorphism, then J=θ⁡(1)​D. Hence D is a principal ideal domain and I is prime.Conversely, every nonzero ideal of a principal ideal domain is isomorphic to the regular module, since it is generated by one element. Thus R/𝔭 is isosimple as an R-module. For every N≤Sn, the action factors through D, and the submodule theorem for free modules over a PID gives N≅Dr with r≤n. See [11] for this standard theorem. The proof also shows why no Noetherian assumption on the original ring R is needed: it is the faithful quotient R/annR⁡(S), not R itself, that must be a PID.Example 2.2.
For any commutative ring R, every prime quotient that is a PID gives a positive example. This includes residue fields, polynomial quotients isomorphic to k⁡[t], and quotients isomorphic to a discrete valuation ring. In particular, over k⁡[x1,…,xd], the module obtained from a surjection onto k⁡[t] has isoartinian finite powers. 4Affirmative cases over noncommutative rings
In this section, we will investigate when the square S2 is isoartinian provided that S is an isosimple module over a non-commutative ring.
4.1Quasi-projective modules and matrix rings
Recall that S is quasi-projective if for every submodule U, every map S→S/U lifts through the natural map S→S/U. We use this definition rather than a projectivity assumption over the original ring. For the general theory see [16, 17]; the standard distinctions between projectivity and quasi-projectivity are also discussed in [11].Theorem 4.1.
If an isosimple module S is quasi-projective, then every submodule of Sn is isomorphic to a finite direct sum of copies of S. In particular, all finite powers of S are isoartinian.Proof.
Proceed by induction on n. Let N≤S⊕Sn−1, let U=N∩(S⊕0), and let V be the image in Sn−1. By induction V≅Sr. If U=0, then N≅V. Otherwise U≅S.There is a well-defined homomorphismh:V⟶S/U,h⁡(v)=s+Uif ​(s,v)∈N.Write V=V1⊕⋯⊕Vr, with each Vi≅S. Quasi-projectivity lifts each restriction h|Vi to a map Vi→S. Adding these lifts gives h~:V→S. Then v↦(h~​(v),v) is a section of N→V, and N≅U⊕V. The case U=S is included, with S/U=0. Proposition 1.4 finishes the proof. ∎Corollary 4.2.
The conclusion holds for simple modules and for projective isosimple modules. A quasi-injective isosimple module is simple, so it also has the conclusion.Proof.
Simple modules are quasi-projective, since their only quotients are themselves and zero. Projective modules are quasi-projective. If S is quasi-injective and 0≠U≤S, an isomorphism U→S extends to an endomorphism of S. It is surjective, hence injective, so its restriction being onto forces U=S. ∎The last observation agrees with the corresponding result for quasi-injective virtually semisimple modules in [4].Proposition 4.3.
An equivalence of module categories preserves isosimplicity, isoartinianity and quasi-projectivity. Consequently, if D is a principal right ideal domain and A=Mt​(D), the standard row module D1×t is isosimple and all of its finite powers are isoartinian.Proof.
An equivalence is exact, preserves finite sums, and induces an order-isomorphism between the subobject lattices of corresponding objects. It preserves isomorphisms and the lifting property defining quasi-projectivity. This proves the first assertion. The usual Morita equivalence between D and Mt​(D) sends DD to the row module. Every right ideal of D is principal and isomorphic to D, and every submodule of Dn is free of rank at most n. These are the standard free-submodule and Morita theorems; see [1, 11]. ∎Example 4.4.
This gives examples from noncommutative division rings and their Ore polynomial rings. If K is a division ring, σ an automorphism and δ a σ-derivation, the ring D=K⁡[x;σ,δ], with x​a=σ⁡(a)​x+δ⁡(a), admits the usual degree division algorithms and is a principal ideal domain on both sides. The row modules over Mt​(D) therefore satisfy Proposition 4.3. The relevant division theory is treated in [6, 13].These examples can also be inflated along any surjection R→Mt​(D). The submodules and their homomorphisms do not change when the action is viewed through the quotient. Thus the original ring need not be prime, hereditary or Noetherian. Upper triangular matrix rings mapping onto such a diagonal block give further examples.

And this is where national security gets serious.

There are many reasons why countries restricted foreign companies like BYD. Protecting domestic manufacturers is one. But the bigger question is data, software, surveillance and national security.

Now think about sectors like telecommunications, defence, energy, software and digital infrastructure…

Whoever controls these sectors could potentially influence how a country communicates, operates and grows. In the wrong circumstances, these capabilities could even be misused.

This is why decisions around companies  cannot be based on connectivity or commercial interests alone.

Affordable internet is important. Competition is important. But national security cannot be an afterthought.

India must carefully evaluate who gets access to its critical infrastructure, what data they collect, where that data goes, who controls the software, and what safeguards exist if geopolitical relationships change.

We should welcome global technology. But we must never become so dependent on any one company that our national interests are compromised.

Because in the future, the countries that control their critical technology may also control their strategic independence.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
🚨 ALLEGED CON ARTIST: Who is Louise Lucas? 

Let me share with you the backstory on a self-described "greedy" lawmaker who waged a war on merit, denigrating Asian American parents and families, and is now indicted for illegally selling marijuana and cheating to create "generational wealth" 

The text that indicts Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas in a new Justice Department indictment announced by US Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel against her for alleged money laundering is this one:

💰 “this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

The words she allegedly later said: 
💰 “I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

Lucas is an important window into the choices that everyone faces: whether to advance in life through merit or through cheating. 

Read our coverage of the indictment here: 

'FOR PEOPLE WHO LOOK LIKE ME'
I know the day that I learned the name of Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas: Feb. 18, 2021. 

WATCH the video I've shared her to see Lucas in action.

She was supporting Virginia state Sen. Scott Surovell and other Democratic lawmakers as they waged a wider battle to remove merit-based admissions to America's former No. 1 high school, Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology, and other governor schools. Their bill: HB 2305.

There were some 20 mostly immigrant parents waiting to speak in the online waiting room: parents from India, China and elsewhere, who saw merit as the only path they have to realizing the American Dream and maybe if they were lucky creating "generational wealth."

Lucas wouldn't let the parents speak. I was watching the debate from the waiting room. My son was attending the school at the time, and I was writing about the efforts of parents to challenge the new admissions policy, eliminating the merit admissions test, as racist. 

A federal judge Conrad Hilton later supported the parents and the Coalition for TJ and called the new admissions policy "patently unconsitutional" and racist.

The ruling was overturned on appeal and the US Supreme Court wouldn't hear the appeal but is now set to hear a similar case from Montgomery County, Md.

Then-state Sen. Chap Petersen was opposing that effort as an effort to target the school's mostly Asian American student population. 

As Petersen spoke about TJ, he noted, “Its population is 80 percent minority.”

Lucas, who is black, interrupted him and said, “Sen. Petersen, for people who look like me, I would appreciate it if you would put a better definition to minority, because I know you’re not talking about people who look like me, so could you please, please be more specific?”

Petersen, whose wife is Korean American woman, said: “The population is about 70 percent Asian.”

Then he added: “People who look like my kids. My kids.” 

Lucas responded: "Mm-hmm."

The war on merit succeeded and TJHSST has plummeted in academic standards and national rankings and is now the FORMER No. 1 high school. Current Virginia Lt. Governor Ghazala Hashmi demonized "parents" and alleged they were racist and supported Lucas and Surovell. 

When Lucas lost the vote, she said: "We will overcome one day."

🔗 This is the full 2018 debate for anyone who wants to see Lucas and her war on merit: https://t.co/w7iGZqXnnW

FAST FORWARD: "GREED" vs. MERIT
Federal prosecutors allege one Lucas, used her political office as part of a years-long operation to sell marijuana, launder the proceeds — and ultimately turn Virginia’s legalization of recreational marijuana into what she allegedly called “generational wealth," not through merit but by allegedly cheating the system.

The 45-page federal indictment names names: 
❌ Louise Lucas
❌ Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke
❌ Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb
❌ Her grandson Ryan Eichelberger
❌ Businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III 
❌ Businessman Carlton Upton Jr.
❌ Businesswoman Tameka Johnson

Prosecutors allege the “Lucas Enterprise” operated from at least 2019 -- two years before the debate on merit -- and pursued two intertwined objectives: 
❌ Distributing marijuana
❌ Using Lucas’ political influence to shape Virginia marijuana policy and obtain valuable recreational licenses

Here is the extraordinary chronology prosecutors laid out, in their own words. 

RISE TO POWER
Lucas was elected to the Virginia Senate in 1991 and rose to become chair of the powerful Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee and Senate President Pro Tempore.

According to the indictment, her family operated The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth.

💰 Her daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly handled business affairs and attended meetings.
💰 Her daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly managed the store.
💰 Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly worked in its day-to-day operations.

Prosecutors say Lucas was explicitly warned.

After a senior law-enforcement officer was hired in 2022, the indictment says he warned Lucas that selling marijuana was illegal and “was going to get her in trouble one day.”

At another meeting, the officer allegedly asked why, “given that she was a state senator and a wealthy woman,” she would engage in criminal behavior.

According to prosecutors, Lucas didn't answer.

By then, prosecutors allege marijuana was already moving through the family business.

2022: 'FREEDOM IS DOPE'
In early 2022, prosecutors say an alleged supplier identified ICC #1 contributed $15,000 to the 420ish Unity Festival, partly organized by Lucas.

The receipt allegedly described the payment as:

“Freedom is Dope.”

Then, on April 19, 2022, Lucas and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke allegedly met ICC #1 at Lucas’ office.

The indictment says that between June and July 2022, an alleged supplier identified as ICC #1 delivered between THREE AND FIVE POUNDS of marijuana to The Cannabis Outlet.

Lucas allegedly paid between $3,500 and $4,000 IN CASH.

'VIRGINIA FREEDOM LIFE'
According to the indictment, Lucas asked ICC #1 whether he was a member of law enforcement before discussing marijuana prices.

That same day, daughter Lucas-Burke allegedly wrote a $6,600 check to ICC #1 from Virginia Freedom Life.

It bounced.

Lucas allegedly replaced it with another $6,600 check from Backyard Entertainment.

By fall 2022, prosecutors allege the business was operating at scale.

Between fall 2022 and early 2023, ICC #2 allegedly sold The Cannabis Outlet “multi-pound quantities of marijuana totaling approximately 100 pounds” for $100,000-$150,000.

Prosecutors say Lucas, through daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb, paid $52,000 in checks and the remainder IN CASH.

Then came the texts.

'THE LUCAS LADIES'
On Oct. 3, 2022, prosecutors say Lucas texted the alleged supplier:

“Good morning … this is to confirm the time for our meeting at the store today. I am so excited and looking forward to seeing you”

And:

“we (The Lucas Ladies) love doing business with you”

'I'M GOING TO NEED MORE FLOWER'
Daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly texted with the supplier about the mechanics of marijuana sales.

One message described packaging and selling “half ounces (14)” and “ounces (28).”

Another allegedly said:

“you can keep going on the blend if you can’t keep up with sativa and indica.”

Days later:

“Good morning. I’m going to need more flower.”

The money trail continued.

The indictment lists payment after payment from The Cannabis Outlet to Prince Albert William Hudson III, whom prosecutors describe as a marijuana supplier.

💰 December 2023: more than $21,000.
💰 January 2024: more than $26,000.
💰 February: more than $29,000.
💰 March: $129,000.
💰 April: $132,000.
💰 May: $125,000.
💰 June: $123,000.
💰 July: more than $79,000.
💰 August: $91,000.
💰 September: $67,000.

And investigators weren't merely watching.

💰 On Oct. 4, 2024, and Oct. 18, 2024, the indictment says law enforcement made CONTROLLED PURCHASES of marijuana from The Cannabis Outlet.

More controlled buys followed.

💰 On May 5, 2025, an undercover officer allegedly bought 10.2 grams of marijuana from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 By 2025, prosecutors allege payments continued flowing to Hudson and another alleged supplier, ICC #1.

The indictment records tens of thousands of dollars month after month.

Meanwhile, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb allegedly received a series of $2,500 payments from an Agri-Carter account controlled by Hudson.

Then investigators intercepted a shipment.

On Aug. 13, 2025, Norfolk police seized SEVEN POUNDS OF MARIJUANA allegedly shipped to High-N-Wellness in Norfolk.

According to prosecutors, payments and marijuana transactions nevertheless continued.

By October 2025, law enforcement was buying directly from The Cannabis Outlet again.

💰 Oct. 23, 2025: controlled purchase of ½ ounce.
💰 Oct. 31, 2025: controlled purchase of one ounce.

During that transaction, prosecutors say Eichelberger told the undercover officer another load of “product” was due Nov. 3.

'THE ELECTION' 
Then came a text prosecutors put directly into the indictment.

On Nov. 15, 2025, Lucas allegedly wrote about “the election” and told ICC #2:

“you know I will be carrying the legislation as the Chief Co-patron.”

She allegedly proposed sitting down to discuss “how about we begin with you sending at least a good faith payment of the money you owe me…”

'LIST OF STUFF FOR YOU TO TRY'
In January 2026, prosecutors say the operation moved directly into Lucas’ legislative office.

Grandson Ryan Eichelberger allegedly began texting businesswoman Tameka Johnson asking for “a lil have a list of stuff for you to try & get for next time.”

Then: “can you get the COAs for the flower and other products?”

💰 On Jan. 30, 2026, according to prosecutors, Lucas asked ICC #2 to come to her office at the Capitol complex in Richmond.

💰 There, the indictment says Lucas provided “partial repayment” of money ICC #2 had paid for an interest in Mama’s Chicken, LLC.

💰 Then Lucas allegedly asked ICC #2 to provide marijuana “samples.”

💰 The next day, Jan. 31, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas and ICC #2 met AGAIN — this time at her legislative office in Portsmouth.

Lucas allegedly called in daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke and grandson Ryan Eichelberger.

They discussed sources of marijuana.

When Eichelberger asked whether the cannabis was hemp, prosecutors say ICC #2 replied:

“[I]t’s not hemp, it’s THC.”

'GET GENERATIONAL WEALTH'
Then prosecutors allege Lucas explained the endgame.

After the conversation, Lucas and ICC #2 allegedly continued discussing marijuana and marijuana licensing.

According to the indictment, Lucas said obtaining a license was a way for her to:

“get generational wealth and this is my last chance.”

The alleged undercover operation kept going.

💰 Feb. 3, 2026: ICC #1 allegedly arrived at The Cannabis Outlet with “a large bag” from his vehicle and took it inside.

💰 Feb. 5, 2026: controlled purchase of 69.5 grams from The CBD Shoppe.

💰 Same day: controlled purchase of 116 grams from High-N-Wellness.

💰 On Feb. 9, 2026, prosecutors say Lucas called ICC #2 and discussed the recreational-marijuana legislation pending in the General Assembly.

The indictment quotes Lucas:

“this is our last chance at generational wealth . . . I’ve got too old to not be greedy.”

Two days later, law enforcement allegedly observed ICC #2 throwing a white trash bag into a dumpster.

Investigators recovered it.

The indictment says the bag contained marijuana packaging bearing “the odor of marijuana.”

March 2026: prosecutors allege the political and business sides increasingly converged.

Lucas allegedly told grandson Eichelberger and businesswoman Tameka Johnson to find additional marijuana sources.

Then, prosecutors say, Lucas telephoned another Virginia legislator and explained why she needed a marijuana license.

The alleged quote is stunning:

“I got to get the license and I got to get the money rolling because I want — I want to make generation, create some generational wealth.”

She allegedly continued:

“I need to be covered under his (UPTON’s) um, hemp license.”

On March 11, 2026. prosecutors say Lucas participated in another call with Virginia legislators and daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke about recreational marijuana licenses.

Lucas allegedly said:

“we trying to disqualify somebody [UCC #2] until he pays me back my money.”

March 31, 2026: Businessman Carlton Upton Jr. allegedly met Lucas at her Portsmouth office.

According to the indictment, Upton told Lucas:

“I only got five licenses, but you know what I mean, you first, so I need to talk to you before I make any decisions that affect you.”

💰 April 23, 2026: prosecutors say Lucas called a member of the Virginia Cannabis Control Authority and asked whether there was anything the official could do for her.

💰 According to the indictment, Lucas said she needed “to invest in something that — that can help me generate some uh, generational wealth for my family.”

Then came the raids.

💰 May 6, 2026: Federal search warrant at The Cannabis Outlet — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at The CBD Shoppe — marijuana recovered.
💰 Federal search warrant at Hudson’s Exotic World in Danville — marijuana recovered.
💰 July 10, 2026: Law enforcement returned to The Cannabis Outlet for another controlled purchase.
💰 Agents bought two strains labeled “Sativa” and “Indica.” According to the indictment: Both tested positive for marijuana.

The grand jury ultimately charged an alleged racketeering conspiracy involving Lucas, daughter Lisa Lucas-Burke, businessman Prince Albert William Hudson III, grandson Ryan Eichelberger, daughter Theresa Lucas-Lamb and businessman Carlton Upton Jr.

Prosecutors say the alleged enterprise sought to obtain and illegally distribute marijuana AND procure “generational wealth” for its members.

The indictment goes further.

Prosecutors allege the enterprise used business entities to disguise marijuana proceeds and used Lucas’ political influence “to insulate the Lucas Enterprise from state law enforcement actions.”

They also allege her influence was used to pursue marijuana licenses that could financially benefit the enterprise.

Prosecutors describe Lucas as the alleged “leader of the enterprise.”

They accuse her of approving and directing criminal activities, arranging marijuana acquisition and distribution, supervising laundering of marijuana proceeds and using her political influence in an effort to shape Virginia legislation for herself and her family.

The indictment contains EIGHT COUNTS, including allegations involving:

❌ Racketeering conspiracy
❌ Conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana
❌ Money laundering conspiracy
❌ Honest-services fraud conspiracy
❌ Maintaining drug-involved premises
❌ Possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug-trafficking crime
❌ Wire fraud

The charges vary by defendant.

One of the most consequential allegations isn't simply that marijuana was illegally sold.

Prosecutors allege Lucas used her elected office to advance the financial interests of herself, her family and associates as Virginia debated creation of a potentially lucrative recreational marijuana market.

The honest-services count alleges a scheme to deprive Virginians of Lucas’ “intangible right” to her honest services.

The indictment alleges Lucas invested money with ICC #2 in an entity positioned to benefit from marijuana licensing, did not report that interest on required Statements of Economic Interests, and later demanded a partial $100,000 repayment while continuing to work to direct a license to ICC #2.

These are allegations. An indictment is not proof of guilt, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. 

That's the position that Sen. Surovell, the lawmaker who pushed the legislation to remove merit from Virginia's No. 1 high school, is taking as he stands by her in support against the indictments.

The government has now laid out, in extraordinary detail, its theory of how an alleged marijuana business, a family network, money and political power converged over years.

And prosecutors repeatedly return to the phrases they attribute to Lucas herself: creating "generational wealth" by being "greedy."

I hope the telling of this story will give you a wider window into why this case captures not only the crossroads that a politician faces of success through merit or through cheating but also the questions that a nation faces: to go down the path that this lawmaker allegedy supported of shortcuts and dishonor or to choose a path of honor, merit and hard work. 

In 2021, Lucas silenced parents who believed in merit and hard work. 

Today, in 2026, she is facing serious charges for violating "honest-services" laws, money laundering, wire fraud and racketeering.

In which path do you believe?

text:
I asked Grok whether Meta or bots could be behind the Cockroach Janta Party Instagram account gaining 20 million followers in just a few days. Here is the response I received, followed by my own observations.
Yes, it is possible — but it is not yet conclusively proven. The facts are as follows:
The CJP (Cockroach Janta Party) Instagram account (@cockroachjantaparty) was launched around 16–17 May 2026 and crossed 20 million followers (reaching over 22 million) in roughly seven days. This is confirmed by multiple media reports. It overtook the follower counts of established parties like the BJP. There are strong suspicions of bots and fake followers. The unnatural speed of growth and sudden jumps raised questions about artificial engagement.
Some have claimed a large share of the followers came from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Turkey. In response, the founder Abhijeet Dipke released data claiming 94% of the followers are Indian.
Delhi Police and other cyber investigations have reportedly found preliminary evidence that fake accounts and foreign bot networks were used to amplify CJP-related content. They have sought data from Meta, Google and X.
Complaints have also been filed alleging that the account’s location was shifted from the US to Ireland and that the growth pattern was abnormal. A cyber forensic investigation has been demanded.
Regarding possible Meta involvement: Meta recently admitted in meetings with the Indian government that money was paid to boost certain content and that illegal content had been amplified. Some are linking this admission to the CJP case. While the algorithm can organically push viral memes, AI-generated content and Gen-Z anger, the possibility of paid promotion or algorithmic bias cannot be ruled out.
Police investigations are ongoing and more information is being sought from Meta, so clearer details may emerge later.
In short, many people doubt that this was a purely organic viral movement. The combination of bots and Meta’s algorithm or paid boost looks increasingly plausible, especially in light of recent police findings and Meta’s own admissions. However, there is still no public, definitive proof that Meta itself planted bots specifically for CJP followers. The ongoing investigations should provide greater clarity.
My observations:
Is it realistically possible for someone with almost no public profile — a former AAP worker living in America — to launch an Instagram account based on a single remark by the Chief Justice and gain two crore followers in one week without any organised support behind him?
The Chief Justice made the “cockroach” remark on 15 May. The very next day, 16 May, a young man studying in America immediately responded by launching the “Cockroach Janta Party” Instagram account under the name Abhijeet Dipke.
In July, Mumbai-based cyber expert and ethical hacker Parmendra Sharma (@ParmendraSharma), speaking to Navbharat Times, claimed on the basis of technical analysis and data that the CJP Instagram account was actually created in April 2026. It was first started from the US and later shifted to Ireland. He showed screenshots on the channel and filed a complaint through a lawyer with the Delhi Cyber Crime Department, demanding a proper investigation.
Meta, which routinely ignores or delays action against child-abuse content that the law requires it to remove, blocked a video by the Prime Minister of India addressed to the country’s youth for five hours without offering any reason. If it was a genuine technical glitch, why did Meta not detect and fix it immediately and restore the video? Why was the video reinstated only after the government formally complained?
When the Indian government issued a 72-hour notice demanding an apology for the mistake, Meta — if it truly believed it had done nothing wrong — would not have rushed within a few hours to meet the minister and government officials and admit that serious errors had occurred on its side.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

text:
INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). 🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

Statement : CERT-In needs to stop spamming vague and alarming cybersec alerts

October 22, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned about government SMS messages circulated in English and Hindi under the sender ID AD-ARWGOV-S (Screenshot 1 and 2). These messages invoke CSK and CERT-In, advise recipients to keep their devices free of botnets and malware, and ask them to download a free removal tool from https://t.co/mUQthB2Kd9. The screenshots also show repeated messages from the same sender warning of imprisonment and fines for fraudulently obtaining SIMs or telecom services.

The malware advisory provides no finding about the recipient’s device. Yet the linked website tells visitors their device is “probably infected”, while its FAQ says their internet service provider has been notified (Screenshot 3). Receiving a generic SMS or visiting this public webpage does not establish an infection. Presenting general awareness messages this way risks causing needless panic and making recipients believe their devices have been individually identified as compromised.

There are also concerns about M-Kavach 2, one of the recommended tools. Its Google Play listing declares “No data collected”, while its linked Android privacy policy describes collecting device identifiers and installed-app details and transmitting this information for analysis. C-DAC must explain this discrepancy and disclose access, security and retention safeguards. 

CERT-In must immediately correct the website and clearly distinguish general advisories from evidence-based infection alerts. Encouraging software downloads through unsolicited SMS links risks normalising behaviour that scammers exploit. Government-recommended tools must remain voluntary, minimise permissions and data collection, and undergo independent security and privacy audits with published findings.

We urge the nodal ministry, MEITY to redirect its resourses from political censorship towards the cyber security of ordinary Indians.

A private key with the value 4. The private keys of eight certificate authorities run by eMudhra could be worked out by anyone from the public certificates. eMudhra is a Bengaluru company licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) to issue digital signature certificates in India. On 21 October 2026, we wrote to eMudhra, CERT-In and MeitY seeking an incident report, an independent audit, fuller disclosure from CERT-In and a regulatory inquiry. (1/8)

Read More: https://t.co/zaz71nGqII

We have asked eMudhra to publish a complete incident report and to re-verify every key ceremony it has run, including those for the licensed Indian hierarchy. We have also asked it to commission an independent audit by an auditor it has not engaged before, to notify affected subscribers, and to correct its press release. We have asked CERT-In to say when it received eMudhra's report. We have asked MeitY and the CCA to open an inquiry under Sections 28 and 29 of the IT Act and to verify independently that the Indian hierarchy was untouched. (7/8)

For most people, the fix arrives through ordinary updates. Keep your browser, operating system and phone up to date, never click through a certificate warning, and ignore any unsolicited message offering a "certificate fix". If you run a website with an emSign certificate, check whether it chains to the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and replace it before 27 October. If you build software, update every certificate bundle you depend on and rebuild your container images. (8/8)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

eMudhra says its Indian digital signature and eSign businesses are unaffected and run on "completely separate" infrastructure. That assurance rests on eMudhra's own assessment, and eMudhra ran the failed key ceremony itself, with its own script. Section 30 of the IT Act requires Certifying Authorities to use secure procedures, and Section 34 requires them to disclose facts that affect the reliability of their certificates. CERT-In issued an advisory on 21 October but did not say when eMudhra reported the incident. We have found no statement from the CCA. (6/8)
